concepts.topicTitle: Money as a medium of exchange
concepts.label: Money as a Medium of Exchange
concepts.cardText: A person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service. Without money, a shoe manufacturer who wants wheat would have to find a farmer who both sells wheat and wants to buy shoes: both parties must agree to sell and buy each other's commodities. This is the double coincidence of wants, an essential feature of a barter system. Money provides the crucial intermediate step and eliminates the need for it: the shoe manufacturer only needs a buyer for his shoes. Since money acts as an intermediate in exchange, it is called a medium of exchange.

concepts.label: Currency as Money
concepts.cardText: Before coins, Indians used grains and cattle as money, then gold, silver and copper coins. Modern currency, paper notes and coins, is not made of precious metal and has no use of its own. It is accepted as a medium of exchange because it is authorised by the government. In India, the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government, and no other individual or organisation may issue currency. The law makes the rupee a medium of payment that cannot be refused in India, so the rupee is widely accepted.

concepts.label: Demand Deposits and Cheques
concepts.cardText: People deposit extra cash with banks, which keep it safe and pay interest. Since these deposits can be withdrawn on demand, they are called demand deposits. A cheque is a paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the person's account to the person named on it, so payments can be settled without cash, as when M. Salim pays his leather supplier. Since demand deposits are widely accepted as a means of payment, along with currency, they constitute money in the modern economy. Modern forms of money are closely linked to the banking system.

concepts.label: Loan Activities of Banks
concepts.cardText: Banks keep only a small proportion of their deposits as cash, about 5 per cent in India these days, to pay depositors who withdraw money on any day; since only some depositors come on a given day, this is enough. Banks use the major portion of deposits to extend loans. In this way, banks mediate between those who have surplus funds (depositors) and those who need funds (borrowers). Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than they pay on deposits, and this difference is their main source of income.

concepts.label: Credit: Positive Role and Debt-Trap
concepts.cardText: Credit (loan) is an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for the promise of future payment. Salim, a shoe manufacturer, borrows to meet the working capital needs of a festival order, delivers on time, makes a profit and repays: credit plays a vital and positive role. Swapna, a small farmer, borrows from a moneylender for groundnut, but pests destroy her crop; the debt grows and she must sell part of her land. This is a debt-trap. Whether credit is useful depends on the risks in the situation and whether there is support in case of loss.

concepts.label: Terms of Credit and Collateral
concepts.cardText: Every loan agreement specifies an interest rate that the borrower pays along with repaying the principal. Lenders may also demand collateral: an asset the borrower owns, such as land, a building, a vehicle, livestock or bank deposits, used as a guarantee until the loan is repaid. If the borrower fails to repay, the lender can sell the collateral. Megha's Rs 5 lakh housing loan at 12 per cent, repaid in monthly instalments over 10 years, needed salary documents and the house papers as collateral. Interest rate, collateral and documentation, and the mode of repayment together are the terms of credit, which vary between lenders and borrowers.

concepts.label: Variety of Credit Arrangements in Sonpur
concepts.cardText: In Sonpur, Shyamal, a small farmer, once borrowed from a moneylender at 5 per cent a month (60 per cent a year) and now borrows from a trader at 3 per cent a month, but must sell his crop to the trader, who buys it cheaply after harvest. Arun, with seven acres, gets a bank loan at 8.5 per cent a year. Rama, a landless labourer, borrows from her employer at 5 per cent a month and repays by working for him; the only source of credit for the landless is the landowner-employers. Cooperatives, like the Krishak Cooperative, are the other major source of cheap rural credit: members pool resources, and their deposits serve as collateral for a large bank loan.

concepts.label: Formal and Informal Sources of Credit
concepts.cardText: Loans can be grouped as formal sector loans (from banks and cooperatives) and informal sector loans (from moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends). The Reserve Bank of India supervises formal lenders: it checks that banks maintain a minimum cash balance and lend not just to profit-making businesses but also to small cultivators and small borrowers, and banks report their lending to it. No organisation supervises informal lenders: they can charge any interest and use unfair means to recover money. Their much higher interest takes a larger part of borrowers' earnings and can lead to a debt-trap. Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country's development.

concepts.label: Formal and Informal Credit: Who Gets What?
concepts.cardText: In urban areas, 54 per cent of loans taken by poor households come from informal sources, while rich households take only 17 per cent from informal and 83 per cent from formal sources; the pattern is similar in rural areas. The rich get cheap formal credit while the poor pay a lot to borrow. The formal sector still meets only about half of rural people's credit needs. So banks and cooperatives must increase their lending, especially in rural areas, and formal credit must be distributed more equally so the poor can benefit from cheaper loans.

concepts.label: Self Help Groups for the Poor
concepts.cardText: Banks are not present everywhere, and bank loans need documents and collateral; absence of collateral is a major reason the poor cannot get bank loans. Moneylenders lend without collateral but charge very high interest, keep no records and harass borrowers. Self Help Groups organise the rural poor, especially women, into groups of 15-20 who save regularly (Rs 25 to Rs 100 or more) and take small loans from the group at less than moneylenders' rates. After a year or two of regular saving, the group can get a bank loan in its name. The group decides on loans and is responsible for repayment, so banks lend without collateral. SHGs help women become financially self-reliant and discuss social issues.
